A lamp does **not** fill the room with a continuous “beam” that hangs around after the source stops. It constantly **creates new photons**. Each photon travels in a straight line until it hits something—wall, ceiling, floor, a dust particle, your eye—and there it is **absorbed** (its energy becomes a tiny amount of heat).

A typical room is only a few metres across, so the longest possible flight for any photon is  

\[
t_{\max }=\frac{\text{room size}}{c}\approx\frac{3\ \text{m}}{3\times10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}}\approx10^{-8}\ \text{s}.
\]

Thus, the very last photon that could be emitted after you flip the switch reaches a surface and is gone within **nanoseconds**. Human vision integrates light over ~10 ms, so we perceive the change as “instant.”

If you placed an ultra‑fast photodiode at the far wall, it would record a brief nanosecond‑long tail of photons after the switch is opened—exactly what the physics predicts. In empty interstellar space there is nothing to absorb the photons, so they keep traveling for billions of years. The “disappearance” you see is simply the rapid absorption of the last photons, not a magical vanishing of light.
